Dear Sharon Crouch,

 During a review of your medical record I noticed your last blood pressure reading was high. It’s important to control blood pressure to stay healthy and lower your risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney problems.

For most people, a home blood pressure of 134/84 or less is considered at goal.

If you have a home blood pressure monitor, I’d like you to measure your blood pressure 3 times over the next week and send the readings to me in an email.

If you don’t already have one, please buy a blood pressure monitor online or at your local Kaiser Permanente pharmacy. We recommend purchasing a blood pressure monitor with an UPPER ARM cuff, such as the Omron 3 Upper Arm Monitor. Wrist or fingertip devices aren’t accurate. Once you have your upper arm blood pressure monitor, please see step-by-step instructions on how to take your blood pressure at home:

Video: https://kpdoc.org/bphomevideo Handout: https://kpdoc.org/bphome

Please let me know if you have any questions about the blood pressure monitor or how to take your measurements at home.

Dear Member,

Kaiser Permanente is outreaching to all our patients who are tobacco users to provide information about our resources for quitting tobacco. We are here to support you in successfully quitting.

If you have already quit smoking, please reply to this message with your quit date so we can update your medical record. If you want to quit and would like to learn more about the resources we have to help, call 1-866-248-0721.

World No Tobacco Day Quitting smoking isn't easy. It takes time. And a plan. You don't have to stop smoking in one day. Start with day one. Let the World No Tobacco Day on May 31 be your day to start your journey toward a smoke-free life. You'll be joining thousands of people who smoke across the world in taking an important step toward a healthier life and reducing your cancer risk. Go online for more info: http:/ /www.who.int/campaigns/world-no-tobacco-day

Quitting tobacco is the best thing you can do for your health. When you quit, your: o Chance of heart attack and cancer decreases o Lung function increases, breathing and circulation improves o Erectile dysfunction improves, ability to smell and taste increases o Blood pressure and pulse rate drops to normal, and more

Quit Tobacco Resources These are covered benefits for our members.

Individual Counseling Appointment with a Health Educator Have a video appointment with a Health Educator. During this appointment, the Health Educator will provide strategies for quitting, support, and motivation for you to be successful in staying quit. Additionally, you will get information about tobacco cessation medications. To schedule an appointment, call 1-866-248-0721.

Sex: F SSN: xxx-xx-1194 Visit date: 5/24/2023

05/24/2023 - Patient Secure Message in MEDICINE FLU CLINIC (continued) Messages (continued)

Wellness Coaching by Phone Talk with a wellness coach one-on-one over the phone. Your coach can help you develop a smoking-cessation plan and discuss a variety of programs and resources available to you, including medications. The Wellness Coach is free of charge. Call 1-866-251-4514 or go online to schedule your phone appointment. Wellness Coaching

Medications to Help You Quit Tobacco Thinking about quitting tobacco? Tobacco cessation medications can double your chances of quitting smoking. The job of the medications is to relieve you of physical cravings and nicotine withdrawal symptoms that you might experience when you quit (like irritability, anxiety, sleep problems, and/or lack of focus). There are a number of medications that help people quit. Tobacco cessation medications may be pills, like Zyban/bupropion, or nicotine replacement, like the patch and gum or lozenge. To learn more about the types of tobacco cessation medications, click here

Apps Calm and MyStrength Apps: Self-care at your fingertips, at no cost to members. Everyone needs support for total health — mind, body, and spirit. These wellness apps can help you navigate life's challenges, and make small changes to improve your sleep, mood, relationships, and more. Click here for more information: Mental Health and Emotional Wellness Apps

Ginger App Ginger is text-based, emotional support coaching app for Kaiser Permanente members that provides 24/7 access to private, one-on-one, text-based support from behavioral health coaches. It is not clinical therapy. To get started, visit Mental Health and Emotional Wellness Apps

Kaiser Permanente members (ages 18+) are eligible for one 90 day subscription every 365 days. After the 90-day subscription period ends, you will no longer be able to chat with a coach. But you will still have access to your chat history and Ginger's self-care library. Once the subscription ends, you must wait 9 months to activate another 90-day subscription at no cost.

Adding counseling support to help you find other effective quit strategies can increase your chances even more. For information on effective strategies and medications to help you quit tobacco, visit Health Education or call1-866-248-2721 to make a free telephone appointment with a Wellness Coach or Health Educator.

Please reach out directly to your primary care provider with other questions.

Comment: Estimated GFR (eGFR) helps us know how the kidneys are working. eGFR is based on the creatinine blood test result, age, sex, and body size. Monitoring eGFR over time helps us understand changes in kidney function.

Actual kidney function may be better or worse than the estimated GFR because blood creatinine levels are affected by body make up, diet, hydration, genetics, and more.

Multiple eGFR values are used to determine chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages, defined by the following ranges:

eGFR 45 - 59 = Stage 3a eGFR 30 - 44 = Stage 3b eGFR 15 - 29 = Stage 4 eGFR under 15 = Stage 5

Everyone can benefit from caring for their emotional well-being and mental health. We offer a wide range of resources to help you:

 Manage or prevent mental health symptoms and support your emotional well-being and overall health.

 Navigate life’s changes and challenges and bounce back after tough times.

Our self-care information, digital tools, classes, and wellness coaching services can be used alone or together with clinical care.

Learn More

 Tame Stress – Learn about stress, its effects, and positive coping skills to help you manage it.

 Manage Depression – Learn about symptoms and treatment for depression. Watch this video to hear stories from others about depression and recovery.

 Overcome Anxiety – Learn about symptoms and treatments for anxiety.

 Improve Sleep – Learn about lifestyle changes and other treatments for insomnia. Watch this 20-minute video.

 Communicate Effectively – Healthy communication is the foundation to health and happiness. Learn effective ways to communicate and keep your relationships fresh.

Use Our Digital Tools (Apps)

 myStrength – The myStrength app is a cognitive behavioral therapy (thought and behavior change) tool. It’s uniquely designed to provide personal inspiration, build resilience, and strengthen skills for emotional wellness.

 Calm – The popular Calm app helps improve sleep, reduce stress, and manage anxiety.

 Ginger – The Ginger app provides 24/7 access to private, one-on-one, text-based emotional support from behavioral health coaches. Kaiser Permanente members ages 18 and older can register on kp.org to access one 90-day subscription every 365 days. (The Ginger app isn’t yet available to Medi-Cal members.)

Interested in myStrength, Calm, or Ginger? Access these apps here.

 Take a Total Health Assessment and Healthy Lifestyle Program – Based on your answers to our total health assessment, we’ll help you make behavior changes most important to you and your health. Wellness Tools to Help You Thrive | Kaiser Permanente

Attend a Class

Classes are available to help you learn how to manage depression, understand anxiety, manage stress, and improve your sleep.

Contact your local Health Education Department to enroll in our classes.

Talk to a Wellness Coach

Taking care of your total health can help improve your emotional and physical well-being. One-on-one wellness coaching by phone is available at no additional cost to Kaiser Permanente members. Wellness coaches can help you:

 Reduce stress  Improve sleep  Quit tobacco  Eat healthier  Increase activity  Manage your weight

Dear Ms. Sharon F Crouch,

Thank you for contacting us and using the E-visit questionnaire.

My name is N V TORRES MD and I work with your primary doctor Dr. Waller. I’m sorry you’re not feeling well. I’ve reviewed your medical history and your E-visit responses. Based on the information you’ve provided, you most likely have a viral infection. Antibiotics are not needed, as they are not effective in treating viral infections. I’ve prescribed BENZONATATE and PROAIR (ALBUTEROL HFA) to help manage the cough and placing these prescriptions on file. You can pick up the prescription at any Kaiser Permanente pharmacy and review the medications with the Pharmacist. Please go to the pharmacy drop-off desk to have your prescription filled. The prescription will be filled after you check in.

If you prefer to use non-Kaiser Permanente pharmacy, please ask that pharmacy to fax a transfer request for this prescription to the Kaiser Permanente pharmacy.

I also recommend home treatment – these are some options that may help your symptoms:

Use a cough suppressant containing dextromethophan (Robitussin DM, Mucinex DM) Follow dosage instructions listed on the product.

Use cough drops, lozenges, hard candy, or ice chips to soothe irritation and dry, tickling coughs.

Sip warm water or tea with honey.

Avoid secondhand smoke. If you smoke, try to cut back.

If your symptoms get worse, call the Appointment and Advice Call Center at 866-454-8855 to make a video, phone, or in-person appointment.

You can also send an email to your doctor. Your doctor will respond within 2 business days.

Sincerely,

N V TORRES MD

Dear Member,

Kaiser Permanente is outreaching to all our patients who are tobacco users to provide information about our resources for quitting tobacco. We are here to support you in successfully quitting.

If you have already quit smoking, please reply to this message with your quit date so we can update your medical record. If you want to quit and would like to learn more about the resources we have to help, call 1-866-248-0721.

World No Tobacco Day Quitting smoking isn't easy. It takes time. And a plan. You don't have to stop smoking in one day. Start with day one. Let the World No Tobacco Day on May 31 be your day to start your journey toward a smoke-free life. You'll be joining thousands of people who smoke across the world in taking an important step toward a healthier life and reducing your cancer risk. Go online for more info: http:/ /www.who.int/campaigns/world-no-tobacco-day

Quitting tobacco is the best thing you can do for your health. When you quit, your: o Chance of heart attack and cancer decreases o Lung function increases, breathing and circulation improves o Erectile dysfunction improves, ability to smell and taste increases o Blood pressure and pulse rate drops to normal, and more

Quit Tobacco Resources These are covered benefits for our members.

Individual Counseling Appointment with a Health Educator Have a video appointment with a Health Educator. During this appointment, the Health Educator will provide strategies for quitting, support, and motivation for you to be successful in staying quit. Additionally, you will get information about tobacco cessation medications. To schedule an appointment, call 1-866-248-0721.

Sex: F SSN: xxx-xx-1194 Visit date: 5/29/2024

05/29/2024 - Patient Secure Message in HEALTH EDUCATION (continued) Messages (continued)

Wellness Coaching by Phone Talk with a wellness coach one-on-one over the phone. Your coach can help you develop a smoking-cessation plan and discuss a variety of programs and resources available to you, including medications. The Wellness Coach is free of charge. Call 1-866-251-4514 or go online to schedule your phone appointment. Wellness Coaching

Medications to Help You Quit Tobacco Thinking about quitting tobacco? Tobacco cessation medications can double your chances of quitting smoking. The job of the medications is to relieve you of physical cravings and nicotine withdrawal symptoms that you might experience when you quit (like irritability, anxiety, sleep problems, and/or lack of focus). There are a number of medications that help people quit. Tobacco cessation medications may be pills, like Zyban/bupropion, or nicotine replacement, like the patch and gum or lozenge. To learn more visit: Quitting Tobacco

Apps Calm and MyStrength Apps: Self-care at your fingertips, at no cost to members. Everyone needs support for total health — mind, body, and spirit. These wellness apps can help you navigate life's challenges, and make small changes to improve your sleep, mood, relationships, and more. Click here for more information: Mental Health and Emotional Wellness Apps

Headspace Care App Headspace Care is text-based, emotional support coaching app for Kaiser Permanente members that provides 24/7 access to private, one-on-one, text-based support from behavioral health coaches. It is not clinical therapy. To get started, visit Mental Health and Emotional Wellness Apps

Kaiser Permanente members (ages 18+) are eligible for one 90 day subscription every 365 days. After the 90-day subscription period ends, you will no longer be able to chat with a coach. But you will still have access to your chat history and Ginger's self-care library. Once the subscription ends, you must wait 9 months to activate another 90-day subscription at no cost.

Adding counseling support to help you find other effective quit strategies can increase your chances even more. For information on effective strategies and medications to help you quit tobacco, visit Health Education or call1-866-248-2721 to make a free telephone appointment with a Wellness Coach or Health Educator.

Please reach out directly to your primary care provider with other questions.

11/19/2024 - Telephone Appointment Visit in ADULT/FAMILY MEDICINE (continued) Clinical Notes (continued)

History of Present Illness The patient presents with diarrhea for the past month, which she initially associated with wine consumption. Despite discontinuing wine, the diarrhea has persisted. She has attempted to manage the symptoms with Pepto-Bismol and fiber supplements, which have provided some relief. She denies any changes in her long-term medication regimen that could account for the new onset diarrhea. She also reports noticing blood on the toilet paper after wiping, but not in the stool itself.

In addition to the gastrointestinal symptoms, the patient has been experiencing worsening shortness of breath, which she attributes to a diagnosis of asthma. She expresses concern about the possibility of COPD, given the severity of her symptoms. She reports using albuterol for symptom management, but denies recent use of prednisone or other treatments.

Ros: As per HPI

Result Notes

Estimated GFR (eGFR) helps us know how the kidneys are working. eGFR is based on the creatinine blood test result, age, sex, and body size. Monitoring eGFR over time helps us understand changes in kidney function.

Actual kidney function may be better or worse than the estimated GFR because blood creatinine levels are affected by body make up, diet, hydration, genetics, and more.

Multiple eGFR values are used to determine chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages, defined by the following ranges:

eGFR 45 - 59 = Stage 3a eGFR 30 - 44 = Stage 3b eGFR 15 - 29 = Stage 4 eGFR under 15 = Stage 5

Values for eGFR before 05/25/2022 will appear in lab results under "Past results".

SUBJECTIVE: Chief Complaint Patient presents with

  • ESTABLISH NEW PATIENT Nausea x's weeks off and on, diarrhea and now constipated

History of Present Illness The patient, with a significant history of alcohol consumption and smoking, presents with ongoing symptoms of nausea and diarrhea. The patient reports having these symptoms for the past three to four months, despite having quit drinking alcohol three months ago. The patient used to consume a bottle of wine daily and has significantly cut back on smoking. The diarrhea is described as uncontrollable and daily, with the patient fearing an accident. Currently has 2 bowel movements a day which are loose. Dark brown in color, sometimes it is associated bright red blood in stool, but she thinks it is due to straining. Sometimes gets abdominal pain with bowel movements. Also noticed some mucus in her stool. However, the patient reports some control over the diarrhea with fiber.The patient also reports a decreased appetite and loss of taste and smell since having COVID-19 two years ago. Despite the decreased appetite, the patient has gained weight, approximately twenty pounds in a year. The patient also reports experiencing night sweats, fatigue, and lightheadedness.. The patient also has a history of peripheral artery disease, for which she takes aspirin, and an aneurysm. She also reports ongoing shortness of breath with ambulation, able to walk a block. Has ongoing cough with mucus production. The patient continues to be a smoker, cut back to 3 cigarettes/day.

SUBJECTIVE: Chief Complaint Patient presents with

  • BRONCHITIS

History of Present Illness Ms. Sharon, a patient with a history of COPD and emphysema, presents with worsening cough and chest congestion. She reports that her cough has been persistent but has worsened since last Friday. The cough is productive, with green sputum, and is associated with chest pain, particularly when she coughs. She also reports shortness of breath and has been using her inhalers, including a rescue inhaler, every four hours. She denies fever but reports feeling slightly warm. She also reports waking up with severe nausea and experiencing cold sweats, where her entire body becomes wet. She denies any recent sick contacts.

She also reports that she has been trying to quit smoking and has reduced her smoking to two cigarettes in one week. She has picked up smoking patches and plans to start using them. She also reports a history of nausea in the mornings, for which she was prescribed Zofran.

If you use Serevent, Advair, QVAR, Dulera, Pulmicort, Symbicort, Alvesco, Breyna, Wixela or Flovent please do not use any of these 12 hours prior to your test. If you use Combivent or Atrovent please do not use any of these 6 hours prior to your test. If you use Albuterol, Ventolin or Xopenex please do not use any of these 4 hours prior to your test. Welcome You have been referred to the Department of Gastroenterology (GI). Our specialists are dedicated to giving you the best specialty care. This letter contains important information to help you prepare for your procedure .

Before your visit

  • Write down the questions or concerns you would like to discuss during your visit.

  • Bring a list of medications you are taking. Your doctor will go over them with you.

  • Get a copy of your records. Have you been treated for a GI condition outsider Kaiser Permanente? If

so, please obtain and bring those records (i.e. procedure reports, pathology, and consult notes) to your visit.

Scheduling your procedure We have received a referral to schedule you for a screening colonoscopy. Please be assured we are working diligently to get every patient scheduled as quickly as possible and understand the importance of getting you booked for your procedure.

The instructions for your procedure, including the date and time, will be sent to you via secure message or letter. Please keep this information on hand so you can reference it as needed.

Please make sure you have a driver that can bring you to the procedure. Some procedures require additional medications and preparation prior to the procedure. This will be mailed to your home or sent via secure message.

We kindly ask that you do not reach out to your primary care physician's office with procedure scheduling queries as they will not be able to provide specific details about it. If you have any questions or concerns, please contact us at the numbers listed below. We look forward to working with you to improve and effectively manage your health.

History of Present Illness Sharon F Crouch is a 70 Y female with a PMH as stated below who presents today for loose stools x 3 months. She states she has loose stools 3 times a week and not daily. She cannot pinpoint exacerbating factors. She has tried pepto, but causes constipation and blackens her stool. She has also been taking fiber supplement / metamucil capsule which she states helps decrease her loose stools as well. She has also cut up alcohol intake which she states was exacerbating her symptoms. Patient has occasional nausea and a decrease in appetite. She denies abdominal pain, change in stool caliber, BRBPR, melena, vomiting, fever, night sweats, chills. They deny significant weight loss in the past 6-12 months. Patient has decreased tobacco smoking to 3 cigarettes daily. She smokes marijuana on occasion. She denies alcohol. Stools studies WNL as well as TTG.

Last colonoscopy? 8/11/2017 Impression: Polyps x2, hemorrhoids

PART A. COLON, CECUM, BIOPSY: - TUBULAR ADENOMA/VILLOTUBULAR ADENOMA.

PART B. COLON, SIGMOID, BIOPSY: - HYPERPLASTIC POLYP.

Colonoscopy Preparation Using Generic for Colyte (GaviLyte-C)

It is very important that you read these instructions well in advance and follow them completely to ensure a successful exam. It is critical for you to thoroughly clean out your colon, which for most patients is harder than the test itself. Stool remaining in the colon can hide polyps or other abnormalities, and it may cause you to reschedule the procedure and repeat your copay if your colon is not well prepared.

 Prescription: Gavilyte-C and Dulcolax (Bisacodyl) has been filed with the pharmacy call center. Walk in to any Kaiser Pharmacy and request the medication in person. They can fill it while you wait.

7 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE Arrange for your designated driver Your driver will be required to remain at the hospital until you are released.

Check your medications. You should stop taking most ‘blood thinners’ NSAID medications and certain vitamins today. DO NOT STOP taking your daily low dose (81mg) aspirin treatment. Stop taking MAOI Inhibitor Azilect (Rasagiline) See medication instructions on the following page. Call your doctor for questions about medications you are taking.

5 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE for females age 50 and younger only

You are required to have a pregnancy test. Failure to have the test could result in the procedure being delayed or cancelled.

Go to a main hospital lab (Eureka, Morse Ave, or South Sac) to have HCG serum blood test. (Not necessary if you have had a hysterectomy or tubal ligation.)

3 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE STOP eating high fiber foods as of this morning. High fiber foods include salads, seeds, nuts and popcorn

2 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE Daytime- Eat normally during the day, and avoid high fiber foods. Do not drink smoothies, shakes or milk. Avoid drinks that are colored red, purple or orange. Dinner- This dinner will be your last solid food before the procedure. Eat a small dinner.

1 DAY BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE Daytime- When you wake up, start drinking only clear liquids. Drink at least 8oz of clear liquid every hour while you are awake today. M ix Gavilyte (Colyte) with water as directed and refrigerate for later use.

No coffee or alcohol. You may drink water, clear juices, Gatorade, clear soda (sprite), broths, and popsicles. NO RED, ORANGE OR PURPLE. You may have yellow or green Jell-o up until you start drinking the Gavilyte (Colyte).

4pm- Take 2 Bisacodyl (Dulcolax) tablets. If the pharmacy dispensed more than 2 tablets, do not take the additional tablets.

6pm- Begin drinking � gallon (64oz) of Gavilyte (Colyte). Drink about 8oz every 15 minutes. Will take about 2 hours. Shake the Gavilyte (Colyte) container before you pour each glass to ensure the powder is well mixed.

Keep drinking clear liquids until 3 hours before your procedure.. You may have to use the bathroom throughout the night.

D A Y O F Y O U R PROCEDURE

Morning- Five (5) hours before your procedure, take 2 white simethicone (Gas-X) pills then begin drinking the rest of the Gavilyte (Colyte) solution. Drink about 8oz every 15 minutes until the remainder of the solution has been consumed. Take 2 more Gas-X pills after finishing the Gavilyte /Coyte solution. Should take about 2 hours to finish the laxative solution.

You must stop drinking 3 hours before your procedure.

Take any necessary medication with a small sip of water only.

If your appointment is for 7:15am, you will need to get up at 2:15am in order to finish the laxative solution and stop drinking liquids 3 hours before your appointment.

*Frequently asked questions

Q. You have given me a list of foods I cannot eat for 3 days prior to my exam, such as seeds, nuts and salads. What CAN I eat for those 3 days?

A. You can eat any foods you wish, with the exception of those listed in the instructions. Meats, dairy products, most fruits and vegetables are fine. Breads that don’t have visible grains are also fine. Don’t take additional fiber such as Metamucil or Citrucel.

Q. Can I drink coffee while I’m on the clear liquid diet? I’m afraid I will get a headache from lack of caffeine.

A. No, coffee is a very dark liquid. It isn’t on the approved list. If you need caffeine you can try drinking Mountain Dew, which has caffeine in it.

Q. Is the prep going to make my hemorrhoids flare up?

A. This is a possibility. To lessen the effect of multiple trips to the bathroom, you can try wiping with wet wipes instead of toilet paper, or just jump in your shower and rinse off. You can use Preparation H or Desitin while you are doing your prep, but please make sure it’s been washed away before you come in for your exam.

Q. I have an early morning appointment. Can’t I just drink my whole prep the night before?

A. No. To have the best possible chance of your colon being clean for the exam, part of the prep needs to be done much closer to your appointment time. If you can’t get up 5 hours before your arrival, maybe it would be better to schedule a later appointment to accommodate your sleep schedule.

Q. What do I need to remember on the morning of my appointment?

A. Be sure to follow the instructions about how to drink the Gavilyte, exactly as provided.

You may take your regular ALLOWED medications on the morning of your appointment.

Please bring a list of all your current medications to your procedure.

Please DON’T wear contact lenses or jewelry. DON’T bring valuables with you. Wear comfortable, loose fitting clothes, and flat shoes or sneakers. On that morning, don’t apply lotion.

You must have a driver bring you and stay during the 2 to 3 hours of your procedure. Unfortunately, we would have to reschedule your appointment if you don’t have a driver

Colonoscopy Procedure Information

The colonoscopy procedure has many applications for different conditions of the colon (large intestine). It can be used to screen the colon for polyps or cancer. It allows for removal of colon polyps, which are growths in the lining of the colon, and allows for taking biopsies (taking samples of tissue) from abnormal areas in the large intestine. Using colonoscopy, the physician can also find sources of bleeding in the colon, may cauterize such areas to control the bleeding, and may locate areas of narrowing or inflammation.

The colonoscopy procedure: A thorough bowel cleaning is needed before the procedure. It is very important to follow the instructions completely to achieve the best results.

On the day of the procedure, the nurse will insert an intravenous (IV) catheter in your arm or hand to allow for the administration of medications to relax you and keep you comfortable before and during the procedure. You will have continuous monitoring of your heart, blood pressure, and breathing throughout the procedure and during the recovery period. The physician then inserts the instrument, which consists of a thin flexible tube with a light and camera at its tip, through the anus and advances it carefully to see the lining of the entire large intestine. After the procedure, you will be monitored in the recovery area for about 30 minutes. It is common to feel some bloating or mild cramping in the abdomen after the procedure due to air that was introduced in the colon during the procedure. You will feel better when you pass the air. Since the sedative and pain medications stay in your system for several hours, it is unsafe and illegal for you to drive until the next day. You will need a driver to take you home after the procedure and the nurses need to be certain of who your driver is prior to the start of the procedure.

The risks or possible complications of the colonoscopy include the following: The risk of perforation or causing a tear in the lining of the colon, which would require hospitalization and surgery to repair the tear. Risk of bleeding from the site of a biopsy or polyp removal, or due to stretching of a narrowed area. This bleeding may also require hospitalization and blood transfusions. An adverse reaction to medications given during the procedure including: allergic reaction to the medications, slowing or stopping of the breathing, lowering of the blood pressure or slowing of the pulse, nausea or vomiting, inflammation of the vein where the catheter was inserted. Abdominal cramping or pain that could last for a few hours until you pass the air. The possibility of missing a polyp or small tumor or small area of inflammation in the lining of the colon. There is a small chance that the doctor may not be able to complete the procedure due to the shape of the colon.

For additional information regarding the procedure(s) you will be having, please visit http://kp.org/mydoctor. Select your physician by name, and click on - Prepare for your procedure* or to view video, select GI

Targeted sonographic evaluation of the breast(s) performed by the sonographer and/or attending physician. Attending physician chaperoned by the sonographer. COMPARISON: Mammograms 1/7/2025, 7/27/2022, 10/21/2019, 7/11/2017, 6/9/2017 (accession 11212507104), Mammogram 1/22/2025 (accession 11212507109) ** FINDINGS **: MAMMOGRAM: Breast composition: There are scattered areas of fibroglandular density.

On additional diagnostic views with 3-D tomosynthesis, there is a tiny persistent circumscribed mass with areas screening mammogram concern. Ultrasound will be obtained for further evaluation.

ULTRASOUND: The patient was scanned by the technologist. In the left breast at 12:00, 6 cm from the nipple at the site of mammographic concern, there is a 0.4 x 7.4 x 0.3 cm minimally complicated cyst/acorn cyst or less likely an unremarkable intraparenchymal lymph node without color flow to hilum due to small size and deep location. No suspicious masses are identified. Impression: BI-RADS 2: Benign RECOMMENDATION: Mammographic screening per KP national clinical practice guidelines. Results were discussed directly with the patient by the radiologist or radiology staff. ---PATIENT INFORMATION--- We're pleased to inform you that your recent imaging exam shows no signs of breast cancer. History of Present Illness Sharon F Crouch is a 71 Y female scheduled to address TEST RESULTS (PFT ) and BLOOD PRESSURE PROBLEM .

History of Present Illness

The patient, with a history of COPD and asthma, presents with persistent nausea, fatigue, and difficulty breathing. The patient reports feeling "winded" in the mornings and has been trying to walk around the block once or twice a day, but has been feeling unwell. The patient has been experiencing nausea for the past couple of weeks, initial symptoms started after Christmas which has been severe at times, and has been associated with a lack of appetite and a change in taste perception. The patient also reports having diarrhea, describing it as severe and frequent, and has been using Metamucil to manage it. The patient is a current smoker and is trying to quit, currently smoking about three cigarettes a day. The patient also uses marijuana, which she believes helps with her appetite. The patient is scheduled for a colonoscopy due to the ongoing diarrhea.

Colonoscopy Preparation Using Generic for Colyte (GaviLyte-C)

It is very important that you read these instructions well in advance and follow them completely to ensure a successful exam. It is critical for you to thoroughly clean out your colon, which for most patients is harder than the test itself. Stool remaining in the colon can hide polyps or other abnormalities, and it may cause you to reschedule the procedure and repeat your copay if your colon is not well prepared.

 Prescription: Gavilyte-C and Dulcolax (Bisacodyl) has been filed with the pharmacy call center. Walk in to any Kaiser Pharmacy and request the medication in person. They can fill it while you wait.

7 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE Arrange for your designated driver Your driver will be required to remain at the hospital until you are released.

Check your medications. You should stop taking most ‘blood thinners’ NSAID medications and certain vitamins today. DO NOT STOP taking your daily low dose (81mg) aspirin treatment. See medication instructions on the following page. Call your doctor for questions about medications you are taking.

5 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE for females age 50 and younger only

Your MD may have ordered a pregnancy test if there is a chance you could be pregnant. Go to a main hospital lab (Eureka, Morse Ave, or South Sac) to have HCG serum blood test. (Not necessary if you have had a hysterectomy or tubal ligation.)

3 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE STOP eating high fiber foods as of this morning. High fiber foods include salads, seeds, nuts and popcorn

2 DAYS BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE Daytime- Eat normally during the day, and avoid high fiber foods. Do not drink smoothies, shakes or milk. Avoid drinks that are colored red, purple or orange. Dinner- This dinner will be your last solid food before the procedure. Eat a small dinner.

1 DAY BEFORE YOUR PROCEDURE Daytime- When you wake up, start drinking only clear liquids. Drink at least 8oz of clear liquid every hour while you are awake today. Mix Gavilyte (Colyte) with water as directed and refrigerate for later use.

No coffee or alcohol. You may drink water, clear juices, Gatorade, clear soda (sprite), broths, and popsicles. NO RED, ORANGE OR PURPLE. You may have yellow or green Jell-o up until you start drinking the Gavilyte (Colyte).

4pm- Take 2 Bisacodyl (Dulcolax) tablets. If the pharmacy dispensed more than 2 tablets, do not take the additional tablets.

6pm- Begin drinking ½ gallon (64oz) of Gavilyte (Colyte). Drink about 8oz every 15 minutes. Will take about 2 hours. Shake the Gavilyte (Colyte) container before you pour each glass to ensure the powder is well mixed.

Keep drinking clear liquids until 6 hours before your procedure.. You may have to use the bathroom throughout the night.

DAY OF YOUR PROCEDURE

Morning- Eight (8) hours before your procedure, take 2 white simethicone (Gas-X) pills, then begin drinking the rest of the Gavilyte (Colyte) solution. Drink about 8oz every 15 minutes until the remainder of the solution has been consumed. It should take about 2 hours to finish the laxative solution. Take 2 more Gas-X pills after finishing the Gavilyte/Colyte solution.

You must stop drinking 6 hours before your procedure.

Take any necessary medication with a small sip of water only.

If your appointment is for 3:15pm, you will need to get up at 7:15am in order to finish the laxative solution and stop drinking liquids 6 hours before your appointment.

Q. You have given me a list of foods I cannot eat for 3 days prior to my exam, such as seeds, nuts and salads. What CAN I eat for those 3 days?

A. You can eat any foods you wish, with the exception of those listed in the instructions. Meats, dairy products, most fruits and vegetables are fine. Breads that don’t have visible grains are also fine. Don’t take additional fiber such as Metamucil or Citrucel.

Q. Can I drink coffee while I’m on the clear liquid diet? I’m afraid I will get a headache from lack of caffeine.

A. No, coffee is a very dark liquid. It isn’t on the approved list. If you need caffeine you can try drinking Mountain Dew, which has caffeine in it.

Q. Is the prep going to make my hemorrhoids flare up?

A. This is a possibility. To lessen the effect of multiple trips to the bathroom, you can try wiping with wet wipes instead of toilet paper, or just jump in your shower and rinse off. You can use Preparation H or Desitin while you are doing your prep, but please make sure it’s been washed away before you come in for your exam.

Q. I have an early morning appointment. Can’t I just drink my whole prep the night before?

A. No. To have the best possible chance of your colon being clean for the exam, part of the prep needs to be done much closer to your appointment time. If you can’t get up 5 hours before your arrival, maybe it would be better to schedule a later appointment to accommodate your sleep schedule.

Q. What do I need to remember on the morning of my appointment?

A. Be sure to follow the instructions about how to drink the Gavilyte, exactly as provided.

You may take your regular ALLOWED medications on the morning of your appointment.

Please bring a list of all your current medications to your procedure.

Please DON’T wear contact lenses or jewelry. DON’T bring valuables with you. Wear comfortable, loose fitting clothes, and flat shoes or sneakers. On that morning, don’t apply lotion.

You must have a driver bring you and stay during the 2 to 3 hours of your procedure. Unfortunately, we would have to reschedule your appointment if you don’t have a driver

Colonoscopy Procedure Information

Sex: F SSN: xxx-xx-1194 Visit date: 2/12/2025

02/12/2025 - Patient Secure Message in GASTROENTEROLOGY (continued) Messages (continued)

The colonoscopy procedure has many applications for different conditions of the colon (large intestine). It can be used to screen the colon for polyps or cancer. It allows for removal of colon polyps, which are growths in the lining of the colon, and allows for taking biopsies (taking samples of tissue) from abnormal areas in the large intestine. Using colonoscopy, the physician can also find sources of bleeding in the colon, may cauterize such areas to control the bleeding, and may locate areas of narrowing or inflammation.

The colonoscopy procedure: A thorough bowel cleaning is needed before the procedure. It is very important to follow the instructions completely to achieve the best results.

On the day of the procedure, the nurse will insert an intravenous (IV) catheter in your arm or hand to allow for the administration of medications to relax you and keep you comfortable before and during the procedure. You will have continuous monitoring of your heart, blood pressure, and breathing throughout the procedure and during the recovery period. The physician then inserts the instrument, which consists of a thin flexible tube with a light and camera at its tip, through the anus and advances it carefully to see the lining of the entire large intestine. After the procedure, you will be monitored in the recovery area for about 30 minutes. It is common to feel some bloating or mild cramping in the abdomen after the procedure due to air that was introduced in the colon during the procedure. You will feel better when you pass the air. Since the sedative and pain medications stay in your system for several hours, it is unsafe and illegal for you to drive until the next day. You will need a driver to take you home after the procedure and the nurses need to be certain of who your driver is prior to the start of the procedure.

The risks or possible complications of the colonoscopy include the following: The risk of perforation or causing a tear in the lining of the colon, which would require hospitalization and surgery to repair the tear. Risk of bleeding from the site of a biopsy or polyp removal, or due to stretching of a narrowed area. This bleeding may also require hospitalization and blood transfusions. An adverse reaction to medications given during the procedure including: allergic reaction to the medications, slowing or stopping of the breathing, lowering of the blood pressure or slowing of the pulse, nausea or vomiting, inflammation of the vein where the catheter was inserted. Abdominal cramping or pain that could last for a few hours until you pass the air. The possibility of missing a polyp or small tumor or small area of inflammation in the lining of the colon. There is a small chance that the doctor may not be able to complete the procedure due to the shape of the colon.

For additional information regarding the procedure(s) you will be having, please visit http://kp.org/mydoctor. Select your physician by name, and click on - Prepare for your procedure* or to view video, select GI Videos.

Upper Endoscopy (EGD) Procedure Information

The upper endoscopy or Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is a test that allows for the evaluation of the lining of the esophagus, stomach and duodenum by inserting a thin flexible tube with a light and camera at its tip through the mouth to see the lining of these organs. The physician performing this procedure can also take biopsies (taking tissue samples) or treat certain conditions directly through this scope, such as cauterizing a bleeding site, applying rubber bands on bleeding veins of the esophagus, stretching narrowed areas with

Sex: F SSN: xxx-xx-1194 Visit date: 2/12/2025

02/12/2025 - Patient Secure Message in GASTROENTEROLOGY (continued) Messages (continued)

balloons, etc. The EGD procedure: To have the stomach clean for this procedure, you will receive instructions about fasting prior to the procedure. Please, follow the instructions carefully to achieve the best results. On the day of the procedure, the nurse will insert an intravenous catheter in your arm or hand for the administration of medications to relax you and keep you comfortable before and during the procedure. You will have continuous monitoring of your heart, blood pressure, breathing throughout the procedure and the recovery period. The physician may spray your throat with a topical anesthetic to numb the throat and then insert the flexible scope through the mouth into the esophagus, stomach and duodenum. After the procedure, you will be monitored in the recovery area for about 30 minutes. You may feel bloating in the stomach due to air that was introduced during the procedure. You will feel better when you pass the air. Since the sedative and pain medications stay in your system for several hours, it is unsafe and illegal for you to drive until the next day. You will need a driver to take you home after the procedure and the nurses need to be certain of who your driver is prior to the start of the procedure.

The risks or possible complications of the upper endoscopy (EGD) include the following: The risk of perforation or causing a tear in the lining of the esophagus, stomach or duodenum, which would require hospitalization and surgery to repair the tear. Bleeding from the site of a biopsy or polyp removal, or due to stretching of a narrowed area. This bleeding may require hospitalization and blood transfusions. An adverse reaction to medications given during the procedure including: allergic reactions to the medications, slowing or stopping of the breathing, lowering the blood pressure or slowing of the pulse, nausea or vomiting, inflammation of the vein where the catheter was inserted. If vomiting or regurgitation occurs during or following the procedure, this can result in aspiration pneumonia (lung infection), which would require antibiotics and possible hospitalization. Possible sore throat for one or more days after the procedure.

Hello Ms. Crouch,

It was a pleasure to speak with you today about leg pain and peripheral arterial disease (PAD). I've included some more information below, but if you have any other questions please do not hesitate to contact me by reply to this email, or by telephone at the numbers below.

Some important points to remember are:

PAD is a condition that is managed, not cured. If you smoke, stopping smoking is critical to success. Surgery for PAD of the legs has more risks associated with it than an exercise program. If you have been diagnosed with PAD and have pain in your feet (not your leg) even when not exercising, or have wounds of the foot that don't heal, contact your doctor.

Further below is some additional information for you to look at and review.

Peripheral Arterial Disease of the Leg

Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) occurs when the blood vessels (arteries) that supply blood to areas of the body become narrowed, reducing flow. The legs are affected most often. Fatty calcified buildup (plaque) in the arteries usually is the cause of PAD. This buildup is called atherosclerosis, sometimes known as "hardening of the arteries". Your risk of PAD increases if you smoke or have high cholesterol, high blood pressure, diabetes, or a family history of PAD. It is also commonly associated with CAD (coronary artery disease) which is blockages in the arteries feeding your heart.

One of the main symptoms of PAD is intermittent claudication. This is a tight, aching, or squeezing pain in the calf, thigh, hip or buttock that occurs during exercise (walking) . The pain usually gets worse during walking and goes away when you rest. Pain in the calf, knee, thigh or buttock at times of rest is almost never related to a vascular issue. However, as PAD gets worse, you may feel pain come on at shorter intervals. Rarely, it can progress further to pain in your forefoot even at rest or non healing ulcers on your feet. If you have been diagnosed with PAD and develop pain in your foot when not exercising, or have sores on your foot that won't

Sex: F SSN: xxx-xx-1194 Visit date: 2/21/2025

02/21/2025 - Patient Secure Message in VASCULAR SURGERY (continued) Messages (continued)

There is no "cure" for PAD. Most patients have options for managing PAD. Most importantly with medical therapies, though this can be combined with endovascular interventional techniques, surgical and nonsurgical techniques. Many patients who have PAD in one region of the body also have arterial disease in other areas of the body, and should be aware of this, but in the absence of symptoms, probably do not benefit from further testing.

Managing PAD without surgery

Do not smoke. Smoking can make PAD worse. If you need help quitting, talk to your primary care doctor about stop-smoking programs and medicines. These can increase your chances of quitting for good.

Take your medicines exactly as prescribed. Good control of any associated medical conditions is critical to your overall care and managing PAD. If you have diabetes, it is particularly important to have tight control of your blood sugars.

Call your doctor if you think you are having a problem with your medicine.

A daily graded exercise program is vital. While exercise of any kind is generally beneficial, exercise for PAD should try to reproduce the discomfort in your legs - walking is usually the best way to do this. The pain in your legs is created by a lack of oxygen in the muscle due to insufficient blood flow. This environment encourages blood vessel dilation. The goal of exercise therapy for PAD is to encourage the development of these small extra blood vessels to the affected area, called "collateral circulation". You should walk until you notice that you have reproduced the pain and then continue through the pain until you can't continue due to the discomfort. At this point, stop and rest, and resume walking until you can't continue - repeating this cycle during the time period of exercise. The more you exercise, the better off you will be. This should be a graded exercise program where you increase your walking distance each month and, if you can, add in some walking on an incline.

Also, if you ever stop the walking program, your symptoms can return to where they were after the progress was made. This is much like any athlete who stops training. One of the more common scenarios is when someone gets an illness and stops their walking program for a couple of weeks. They will notice their walking distance has become much shorter when they re start walking. Take good care of your feet. Treat cuts and scrapes on your legs right away. Poor blood flow can slow or prevent quick healing of even small cuts or scrapes. This is even more important if you have diabetes. Avoid shoes that are too tight or that rub your feet. Shoes should be comfortable and fit well. Avoid socks or stockings that are tight enough to leave elastic-band marks on your legs. Tight socks can make circulation problems worse. Keep your feet clean and moisturized to prevent drying and cracking. Place cotton or lamb's wool between your toes to prevent rubbing and to absorb moisture if you are susceptible to skin cracking. If you have a sore on your leg or foot, keep it dry and cover it with a nonstick bandage until you see your doctor.

Managing PAD without surgery is often the safest option for most patients. These methods are not expected to lead to large improvements in your walking ability, but often will produce a noticeable improvement and do not expose you to the risks involved with surgery for PAD, which can include an increased risk of requiring an amputation in the future, compared with patients who are able to stop smoking and stay on an exercise program.

02/21/2025 - Patient Secure Message in VASCULAR SURGERY (continued) Messages (continued)

Surgery for PAD

Surgery for PAD is best reserved for those patients who have pain at rest or non-healing wounds. Surgery is sometimes offered to patients with severe claudication who feel that their lifestyle is so limited by their PAD that they are willing to accept the risks of surgery. Active smokers are poor candidates for vascular surgery due to increased risks of surgical complications and increased risk of failure of interventions.

Surgery for PAD may involve procedures done through catheters threaded into the vessels themselves ("endovascular" techniques), or may involve bypassing the arterial blockages with new implanted artificial arteries or the use of your own veins as a conduit. Most patients will need to have an arteriogram before the discussion of which procedure is the right one for them. An arteriogram is a test usually done in the Interventional Radiology (IR) suite, where a small catheter is threaded through an artery in the groin into the aorta, dye is injected into the arteries, and a series of x-ray pictures are taken to see where the blockages are, and what would be required to overcome them.

The risks of having vascular surgery procedures, including arteriograms and endovascular interventions and open operations, include risks of anesthesia (such as heart attack or stroke under anesthesia), injury to blood vessels, bleeding, infection, clot formation, distal embolization (having small bits of plaque break off and lodge in smaller arteries), allergic reaction to the dye, and the possibility of the dye being damaging to the kidneys, which can cause decrease in function or failure of, the kidneys. Rarely, complications of procedures makes PAD worse through one of these processes, and can even accelerate limb loss (amputation). All vascular interventions and open bypass operations are at risk to fail over time, and require some type of surveillance and sometimes require re-intervention in the future. This is why patients who have surgery for PAD can be at some added risk of amputation at some point than patients who are managed medically, abstain from smoking and maintain an graded exercise program.

All open and endovascular interventions are aided by taking good care of any of your medical problems such as diabetes, hypercholesterolemia (high cholesterol), hypertension and smoking cessation.

I understand that this is a lot of complicated information and encourage you to discuss your specific situation with me or your doctors as you feel you need.

Sincerely,
